newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia seen producing record canola crop.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia seen producing record canola crop.

text.p: Australia is set to produce another record canola crop in 1997/98 as growers respond to still relatively favourable returns, The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said on Tuesday.
However, ABARE said world oilseed prices were expected to fall in 1997/98 (June 30) as production expanded and stocks rose.

ABARE, the Australian government's main commodities forecasting agency, said it expected Australia to produce about 2.017 million tonnes of oilseeds in 1997/98, up 18 percent from expected output of 1.710 million tonnes in 1996/97.

Within the total canola production was expected to rise to 822,000 tonnes, a 33.4 percent increase from an expected 616,000 tonnes in 1996/97. Australia produced 1.403 million tonnes of oilseeds in 1995/96, including 561,000 tonnes of canola.
However, ABARE said it expected the world indicator price for soybeans (CIF Rotterdam) to fall 10 percent in 1997/98.
This would reflect increased production and an expected recovery in world stocks, ABARE said.
"In 1997/98, the world stocks to use ratio is forecast to rise to five percent from four percent in 1996/97," it said.
ABARE said world oilseeds production was expected to rise four percent as producers continue to boost the area sown to oilseeds, particularly soybeans, canola and sunflowers.
World oilseeds demand was expected to increase further in 1997/98, the forecaster said.

"In the developed countries, lower oilseeds prices relative to meal and oil are expected to boost processing margins and stimulate intake," it said. "In addition to this Asian processor and import demand is expected to be encouraged by continued strong growth in the demand for meal and oil products."
However, it said China's import demand for soy products and soybeans was expected to fall in 1997/98 as domestic oilseed output recovered from a relatively small 1996/97 harvest.
ABARE said world vegetable oil prices were expected to remain stable in 1997/98 as continued growth in population and incomes results in increased vegetable oil consumption.
"Demand growth is expected to be strongest for palm oil as income growth stimulates food demand throughout Asia, where palm oil is the traditional cooking oil," ABARE said.
"However, higher income consumers in Asia are expected to continue to move away from palm oil and into higher quality oils produced from oilseeds such as soybeans and canola," it said.
